column2: Applying economic reasoning to business decisions
column3: A manager comparing alternative uses of scarce factory capacity is applying economic reasoning to a business decision.
column4: Business economics assumes that resources are unlimited whenever a firm seeks profit.

column2: The value of the best alternative sacrificed
column3: If a shop used by its owner could earn Rs 20,000 monthly rent, using it personally has that forgone rental opportunity cost.
column4: An owner-occupied shop has no opportunity cost merely because no rent cheque is paid.

column2: Revenue minus explicit and implicit opportunity costs
column3: Revenue Rs 5 lakh, explicit costs Rs 3 lakh and implicit costs Rs 1 lakh imply Rs 1 lakh economic profit.
column4: The same figures imply Rs 2 lakh economic profit because implicit costs are never deducted.

column2: Revenue minus recorded explicit expenses
column3: Positive accounting profit can coexist with zero economic profit when implicit opportunity costs absorb the recorded surplus.
column4: Positive accounting profit always proves positive economic profit.

column2: The minimum return included in economic opportunity cost
column3: Zero economic profit can include compensation sufficient to keep the entrepreneur in the activity.
column4: Zero economic profit means the entrepreneur must receive absolutely no return.

column2: Choosing output to maximise the difference between total revenue and total cost
column3: For an interior optimum, MR equals MC and MC must cross MR appropriately; equality alone is not sufficient.
column4: Every MR-MC intersection is a profit maximum regardless of the curves' behaviour.

column2: Choosing output to maximise revenue subject to relevant constraints
column3: Without a binding profit constraint, an interior total-revenue maximum occurs where MR is zero.
column4: Without a binding profit constraint, total revenue is maximised whenever price is zero.

column2: Quantity demanded generally varies inversely with own price other things equal
column3: An own-price fall produces a movement along the demand curve when income and other demand determinants remain unchanged.
column4: An own-price fall necessarily shifts the demand curve even when every other determinant is unchanged.

column2: A shift of the demand curve caused by a non-own-price determinant
column3: Higher income shifts demand right for a normal good at each unchanged own price.
column4: Higher income for a normal good is only a movement along its unchanged demand curve.

column2: Responsiveness of quantity demanded to changes in own price
column3: A 10% price rise producing a 20% quantity fall gives an absolute elasticity of 2 using the stated percentage changes.
column4: Those percentage changes imply absolute price elasticity of 0.5.

column2: Demand with absolute price elasticity below one
column3: A small price increase raises total revenue when demand is locally inelastic and other determinants stay unchanged.
column4: A small price increase necessarily lowers revenue when demand is locally inelastic.

column2: Demand with absolute price elasticity above one
column3: A small price reduction raises total revenue when demand is locally elastic and other determinants stay unchanged.
column4: A small price reduction necessarily lowers total revenue when demand is locally elastic.

column2: Demand with absolute price elasticity equal to one
column3: With Q equal to 1,000 divided by P, total revenue is Rs 1,000 at every positive price in the stated curve.
column4: With Q equal to 1,000 divided by P, total revenue increases proportionately with price.

column2: Elasticity calculated at a particular point on a demand curve
column3: For Q = 100 - 2P at P = 20, Q = 60 and absolute point elasticity is 2/3.
column4: For the same demand and price, absolute point elasticity is 3/2.

column2: Elasticity calculated between two points using average price and quantity
column3: Moving from P=10,Q=100 to P=12,Q=80 gives absolute midpoint elasticity 11/9.
column4: The midpoint elasticity for those points is 9/11.

column2: Responsiveness of demand to changes in consumer income
column3: A 10% income rise causing a 5% demand fall implies income elasticity of -0.5.
column4: A 10% income rise causing a 5% demand fall implies income elasticity of +0.5.

column2: Responsiveness of one good's demand to another good's price
column3: Positive cross-price elasticity is consistent with substitutes, holding other determinants constant.
column4: Positive cross-price elasticity necessarily identifies complements.

column2: Goods used together with negative cross-price elasticity in the usual case
column3: A rise in printer prices can reduce demand for printer cartridges, other things equal.
column4: A rise in printer prices necessarily increases cartridge demand merely because they are used together.

column2: A good whose demand decreases as consumer income rises
column3: A good can be inferior without being a Giffen good.
column4: Every inferior good necessarily has an upward-sloping own-price demand curve.

column2: An inferior good whose adverse income effect outweighs substitution after an own-price rise
column3: For a Giffen response, the income effect must dominate the substitution effect in the relevant range.
column4: Every price rise creates a Giffen response whenever the good is inexpensive.

column2: Marginal revenue equals price times one minus inverse absolute elasticity for a downward-sloping demand curve
column3: At price Rs 120 and absolute demand elasticity 3, MR equals Rs 80.
column4: At price Rs 120 and absolute demand elasticity 3, MR equals Rs 160.

column2: Total satisfaction from consumption
column3: If total utility rises from 50 to 58 after one additional unit, the marginal utility of that unit is 8.
column4: The same total-utility change implies marginal utility of 58.

column2: Additional satisfaction generally declines as consumption expands other things equal
column3: Total utility can keep rising while marginal utility is positive but falling.
column4: Falling marginal utility necessarily means total utility is already falling.

column2: Allocating expenditure so marginal utility per rupee is equal across goods at an interior optimum
column3: If MUx/Px exceeds MUy/Py, reallocating some expenditure toward X can increase utility under the standard diminishing-utility assumptions.
column4: If MUx/Px exceeds MUy/Py, utility is improved by reallocating expenditure toward Y.

column2: Combinations of goods giving equal utility
column3: Two indifference curves representing distinct utility levels cannot intersect under consistent preferences.
column4: Distinct indifference curves can intersect while preserving consistent rankings of all bundles.

column2: The amount of one good a consumer will give up for another while utility stays constant
column3: For smooth convex preferences, willingness to give up Y for another unit of X generally falls as X increases along the curve.
column4: Convexity requires willingness to sacrifice Y for X to rise continuously as X increases.

column2: Affordable combinations exhausting income at given prices
column3: With income Rs 200 and Px Rs 20, the X-axis intercept is 10 units regardless of Py.
column4: The same income and Px give an X-axis intercept of 20 units.

column2: The best affordable bundle under the consumer's preferences
column3: At a regular interior tangency, MRS equals Px/Py; corner optima need not satisfy that tangency equality.
column4: Every consumer optimum, including every corner solution, must be a smooth tangency.

column2: The consumption change caused by changed purchasing power from a price change
column3: A price fall raises real purchasing power with nominal income fixed, but the consumption response depends on whether the good is normal or inferior.
column4: A price fall raises nominal money income by definition.

column2: The consumption change caused by changed relative prices with utility or purchasing power compensated
column3: The compensated substitution effect of an own-price fall encourages consumption of the relatively cheaper good under standard preferences.
column4: The compensated substitution effect of an own-price fall always discourages consumption of that good.

column2: The relationship between inputs and technically feasible output
column3: A production function concerns technical transformation rather than the market price paid for output.
column4: A production function alone determines profit without any input or output price information.

column2: Output behaviour when one input varies and other inputs are fixed
column3: Diminishing marginal product can occur while total product still rises if marginal product remains positive.
column4: Diminishing marginal product necessarily implies negative marginal product.

column2: Total output divided by the quantity of a variable input
column3: When marginal product exceeds average product, adding input raises average product.
column4: When marginal product exceeds average product, adding input lowers average product.

column2: Additional output from an additional unit of input
column3: If output rises from 40 to 47 when labour rises by one unit, marginal product is 7.
column4: The same change gives marginal product of 47.

column2: The rational short-run region with positive but diminishing marginal product after maximum average product
column3: Stage II ends where marginal product reaches zero and total product reaches its maximum.
column4: Stage II ends where average product first reaches its maximum.

column2: Output response when all inputs change proportionately
column3: If doubling every input triples output, the technology exhibits increasing returns to scale over that change.
column4: If doubling every input triples output, the technology exhibits diminishing returns to scale.

column2: Output changes in the same proportion as all inputs
column3: For Q = K^0.4 L^0.6, doubling K and L doubles Q.
column4: For Q = K^0.4 L^0.6, doubling both inputs quadruples Q.

column2: Input combinations yielding the same output
column3: Different input mixes on one isoquant produce the same quantity of output under the given technology.
column4: Different points on one isoquant necessarily represent different output quantities.

column2: The rate at which one input replaces another at constant output
column3: For a regular cost-minimising interior choice, MRTS equals the input-price ratio.
column4: An interior cost-minimising choice requires MRTS to equal the output selling price.

column2: Short-run cost that does not vary with output
column3: A fixed factory rental charge is incurred even if short-run output is zero.
column4: Every fixed cost becomes zero whenever short-run output is zero.

column2: Fixed cost divided by output
column3: With fixed cost Rs 1,000, raising output from 100 to 200 lowers AFC from Rs 10 to Rs 5.
column4: With the same fixed cost, doubling output doubles AFC.

column2: The additional total cost associated with an additional unit of output
column3: A change in total fixed cost alone does not shift the marginal-cost curve when variable-cost technology is unchanged.
column4: An increase in fixed cost alone necessarily raises marginal cost at every output.

column2: Total variable cost divided by output
column3: If marginal cost is below AVC, increasing output locally pulls AVC downward.
column4: If marginal cost is below AVC, increasing output locally pushes AVC upward.

column2: A price-taking firm stops production when price is below minimum average variable cost
column3: A firm may produce despite an accounting loss when revenue covers variable costs and contributes toward unavoidable fixed costs.
column4: Any short-run loss requires immediate shutdown regardless of variable-cost coverage.

column2: Falling long-run average cost as scale expands
column3: Economies of scale are a cost relationship, while returns to scale are a technical output-input relationship.
column4: Economies of scale and returns to scale are identical concepts in every context without reference to prices.

column2: A market with price-taking firms selling homogeneous output
column3: A competitive firm faces P=AR=MR for its own output at the market price.
column4: A competitive firm can raise its selling price freely without losing buyers to identical competitors.

column2: A market with one supplier and barriers to entry
column3: A monopolist still faces demand constraints and need not earn positive profit in every possible cost situation.
column4: Monopoly guarantees positive profit regardless of demand and cost.

column2: Competition among many firms offering differentiated products
column3: Long-run free entry can eliminate economic profit while the representative firm has excess capacity.
column4: Long-run zero economic profit necessarily implies production at minimum average cost under monopolistic competition.

column2: A market with few strategically interdependent firms
column3: A price decision can depend on expected rival responses because firms recognise mutual interdependence.
column4: An oligopolist can always ignore rival reactions because there are few rivals.

column2: A pricing arrangement in which other firms follow a leading firm's price
column3: A dominant-firm leader considers residual demand after the competitive fringe's supply.
column4: A dominant-firm leader necessarily faces the entire market demand without accounting for fringe output.

column2: Charging different prices for equivalent output where differences are not explained by cost alone
column3: Separating markets and restricting resale can help sustain discrimination between groups with different demand elasticities.
column4: Unrestricted costless resale between groups always supports sustainable different prices.

column2: Different prices charged to separable customer groups
column3: Under standard interior profit maximisation with equal marginal supply cost, the group with less elastic demand generally faces a higher price.
column4: Under those assumptions, the group with more elastic demand must face the higher price.

column2: A high introductory price aimed at customers with high willingness to pay
column3: A high launch price followed by later reductions illustrates skimming rather than initial low-price penetration.
column4: A high launch price followed by later reductions is necessarily penetration pricing.

column2: A low introductory price intended to build adoption or market share
column3: A low entry price may attract a large customer base but does not itself guarantee long-run profitability.
column4: Penetration pricing guarantees high long-run profit even if variable cost exceeds the selling price.

column2: Different prices by demand period when capacity is constrained
column3: Higher prices at peak demand can help allocate limited capacity; differences need not be due only to different customer identities.
column4: Peak-load pricing requires the product to be sold only to different nationalities.
